name: Kick-off & Planning
obj: Launch the project, align everyone on challenge, scope and roles, and turn the proposal into a Discovery plan.
who: CoDesign team prepares and facilitates · Client project team shares context and constraints · Account team ensures continuity with Presales.
acc: CoDesign lead owns the plan; client sponsor approves scope and governance.
when: Right after project confirmation, before any research.
inputs: Signed proposal, Client Intelligence, existing data, stakeholder list, timeline. Minimum evidence: named sponsor, decision owner and dates.
output: A shared Project & Discovery Plan with RACI (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed).
std: Every research question has an activity, an owner and a date.
quality: Explicit scope and roles; learning-focused plan; realistic activities.
mistakes: Presenting conclusions at kick-off · no decision owner · research questions that are really solutions.
example: HEAL: St Aldric kick-off lists known (waste audit) vs unknown (why families feel excluded); research questions lead to ward shadowing and family interviews; RACI names the dietitian as Consulted for every concept. [fictional]

var.WORK: Northbridge: research questions on anchor-day behaviour; badge data owner named.
var.PLAY: Riverside: matchday observation slots booked around fixtures.
var.LEARN: Lakeshore: timetable data request and student union as Consulted.

cred: Cincinnati Children's materials are internal working documents; confirm sharing rules before showing outside the team.
prompt: 'From this signed proposal [paste], draft the kick-off agenda, a Know / Don't know / Assume table and 6 research questions mapped to Discovery activities.'
verify: Dates, names, scope; remove any 'finding' the AI presents before research.
fallback: Use the 12-heading template: Context → Ambition → Challenge → Know/Don't know → Assumptions → Questions → Activities → Stakeholders → Roles → Governance → Timeline → Next steps.
l_obj: Reframe a kick-off from 'conclusions' to 'learning plan' and match 3 activities to questions.
explain: Presales says what we propose to do; Kick-off turns it into how we will actually do it.

exercise.situation: The proposal is signed. The client team arrives expecting you to present conclusions.
questions: How do you reframe the session in the first five minutes?
List what is known and what must be learned.
Which three Discovery activities would you choose, and what does each answer?

answer_key.sample_answer: Open with the ambition and 'what we must learn to decide well'. Activities: observation (what people do), interviews (why), data review (how often). Each tied to one research question.
answer_key.success_criteria: Each activity answers a named question; nothing presented as a finding.

name: Research & Context Base
obj: Build a shared knowledge base before field research: what is known, assumed and missing.
who: CoDesign team collects and structures · Client provides data and documents · Account team adds history.
acc: CoDesign lead reviews the fact/assumption split.
when: After kick-off, before interviews and visits.
inputs: Kick-off outputs, client studies, surveys, operational data, old personas/journeys. Minimum evidence: each fact cites a document and date.
output: A Context & Knowledge Base: facts, data, users, stakeholders, constraints, assumptions, gaps, questions.
std: Traceable to source; gaps written as research questions.
quality: Focused, evidence-based, connected to the challenge.
mistakes: Copying the whole survey · treating old personas as current · ignoring contradictions.
example: LEARN: Lakeshore's survey says 'affordable' is the top driver; the dashboard shows rising uptake of the cheapest item; the old persona says students 'want healthy options'. Contradiction flagged; question: 'What does affordable mean for a commuter on a work day?' [fictional]

var.WORK: Badge data vs 'nobody comes in on Mondays' assumption.
var.PLAY: Kiosk sales by minute vs complaints by stand.
var.HEAL: Plate-waste audit vs patient satisfaction comments.

prompt: Generic Claude prompt: 'Read these documents [attach]. Build a table Fact / Source / Date / Confidence, then list assumptions, contradictions and 5 research questions. Do not invent data.'
verify: Each fact against its source; no figure without a source.
fallback: Five questions on one Miro frame: What do we know? What evidence? What do we assume? What is missing? What do we investigate?
l_obj: Classify material into fact, assumption and contradiction, and convert the largest gap into a research question.
explain: Know what you know before you go into the field.

templates.label: Project template root (SharePoint) — 01_Discover folder; Context Base template: MISSING, owner Gabriel

exercise.situation: The client sends a 90-page satisfaction survey, two old personas and an operations dashboard.
questions: How do you decide what is worth keeping?
Give one fact, one assumption and one contradiction.
Turn the biggest gap into a research question.

answer_key.sample_answer: Keep what links to the challenge and is recent. A good research question is open and behavioural ('How do commuters decide where to eat between classes?').
answer_key.success_criteria: Fact cites source; research question is open and behavioural.

name: Visit & Interviews
obj: Understand real experience by combining what people say, what they do and what they experience.
who: CoDesign team researches and captures evidence · Client opens access to sites and people · Users and frontline staff share experience.
acc: CoDesign lead approves guides and consent approach; client confirms site rules.
when: Once context and knowledge gaps are known.
inputs: Context Base, research questions, stakeholder map, guides, visit plan. Minimum evidence: at least 2 user types and 1 frontline role; consent recorded.
output: Field findings: observations, notes, quotes, behaviours, needs, pain points, workarounds, constraints, emerging insights.
std: Each finding is tagged observed / said / interpreted.
quality: Diverse perspectives; open, non-leading questions; real behaviour captured.
mistakes: Leading questions · only interviewing managers · mixing interpretation into notes · no consent.
handoff: Debriefed findings → 04.01 Personas and 04.02 Journey Map.
example: WORK: at Northbridge 12:30, observe that teams split into two queues and regroup at tables 15 min later (observed). Team lead says 'lunch is our team meeting' (said). Interpretation: the queue breaks the social moment. [fictional]

var.PLAY: Observe half-time from the concourse; interview a steward and a family.
var.HEAL: Shadow a ward host round; interview a family member with consent and ward approval.
var.LEARN: Observe the library annex at 13:00; interview commuters in the car park area.

cred: Cooper / Cincinnati site-visit playbook referenced on V1 board; confirm shareable version.
tools: Site Visit Playbook, interview guide, observation guide, Plaud/transcription, Miro
prompt: 'Draft a 45-minute interview guide for [user] on [research question]. Open questions only, with 2 follow-ups each, and an observation checklist for [site, time].'
verify: No leading questions; consent and anonymisation; transcripts are not pasted into tools without approval.
fallback: Paper guide: 5 open questions + 'tell me about the last time…' + observation grid (time, place, action, workaround).
l_obj: Rewrite leading questions and record observation, statement and interpretation separately.
explain: Don't only ask people what they need. Observe what they actually do.

templates.label: Project template root (SharePoint) — interview/observation guides and Site Visit Playbook: location TO CONFIRM (Cooper playbook requested in Diane's V1 comment)

exercise.situation: You are observing a staff restaurant at 12:30, with one hour on site and one interview slot with a frontline manager.
questions: What do you watch for that people would never tell you?
Rewrite: 'Don't you think the queue is too long?'
How do you record observation vs statement vs interpretation?

answer_key.sample_answer: Watch workarounds, waiting, who eats alone, trays left. Rewrite: 'Tell me about the last time you had lunch here.' Use three columns or tags: O / S / I.
answer_key.success_criteria: Rewritten question is open and neutral; notes are tagged O/S/I.

name: Benchmark
obj: Learn how others, inside and outside the sector, address similar challenges, and extract transferable principles.
who: CoDesign team researches and curates · Experts suggest references · Client reacts.
acc: CoDesign lead checks sources and the 'so what' of each example.
inputs: Research questions, themes, trend reports. Minimum evidence: every example has a source link and date.
output: A curated Benchmark & Inspiration Landscape with examples, principles and transferable learnings.
std: Each example answers 'so what for this client?'
mistakes: A competitor list with no insight · copying features instead of principles · unsourced examples.
example: PLAY: to cut half-time queues, look at airport fast lanes and theme-park virtual queues; principle: 'move the wait out of the peak'. Benchmark is evidence from elsewhere, not proof it works here.

var.WORK: Co-working spaces' booking of team tables.
var.LEARN: Public libraries that allow food zones.

tools: Benchmark agent, inspiration library, trend reports, web research
prompt: 'Find 8 examples (4 outside [sector]) addressing [challenge]. For each: what they do, why it works, transferable principle, source link and date. Flag anything you could not verify.'
verify: Open every link; check dates; remove examples without a live source.
fallback: Template row: Question → Theme → Example → What they do → Why it works → Principle → Transferability → Opportunity.
l_obj: Extract a transferable principle from an out-of-sector example and defend it to a sceptical client.
explain: Benchmark is not a collection of competitors. Always answer 'So what?'

templates.label: Project template root (SharePoint) — Benchmark template: MISSING, owner Gabriel

exercise.situation: You need inspiration to reduce waiting time in a corporate restaurant.
questions: Name one example from outside food service and why.
What is the transferable principle, not the feature?
How do you answer 'but we are not a theme park'?

answer_key.sample_answer: E.g. airport security lanes: principle 'separate quick and complex transactions'. Answer: 'We are not copying the park, we are borrowing the idea of moving the wait.'
answer_key.success_criteria: Principle stated without the original feature; source named.
